newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians doubt Netanyahu despite handshake.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians doubt Netanyahu despite handshake.

text.p: Benjamin Netanyahu may have broken the ice when he shook hands with Yasser Arafat, but many Palestinians remain sceptical of the right-wing Israeli prime minister's sincerity about making peace.
"Netanyahu met President Arafat under Arab and international pressure. He did not go down to Gaza out of his own will," said Mousa Suleiman, a 34-year-old accountant in Jerusalem.
"Naturally, it is good to see him agree to meet President Arafat, but we have to see how this meeting is going to change things," he said.

Netanyahu and Arafat relaunched stalled Israeli-PLO negotiations when they met and shook hands for the first time on Wednesday at the border between Gaza and Israel. The meeting appeared to calm tensions which had been growing since the Likud party leader ousted Nobel peace prize winner Shimon Peres in Israeli elections in May.

The two leaders agreed to activate a joint steering committee on implementing self-rule accords agreed upon last year. But they failed to set dates for implementing various provisions of the agreement expanding Palestinian self-rule.
Some Palestinians welcomed the meeting as a climbdown by Netanyahu from his previous opposition to shaking Arafat's hand.
But many said the meeting in itself was not sufficient proof of the Israeli government's commitment to peace.
"I do not want to belittle the importance of the meeting, which I regard as the only achievement since the Likud came to power," Legislative Council speaker Ahmed Korei said.

"They must provide something tangible to show goodwill. We still have doubts and we are not convinced that they will commit themselves to implement the agreements and to refrain from settlement activity," he said.

Palestinians had expected Netanyahu to set a date for Israeli army redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron, seen as a test of Israel's commitment to peace. Under the accord, Israel was due to pull out troops from most of Hebron in March.

Palestinians also want Israel to free Arab prisoners still held by the Jewish state, lift a closure imposed during a spate of Islamic suicide bombings in February and March and open a safe passage between the West Bank and Gaza.
They also want Israel to agree to freeze plans to expand Jewish settlements in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.

"We do not see any document to show that a breakthrough had been achieved. The meeting appears to be no more than another attempt (by Israel) at procrastination," said Majeda al-Maani, a 35-year-old Palestinian civil servant in the West Bank town of Nablus.
Muatasem Ahmed, a 34-year-old accountant from Jenin, said: "I am not optimistic. The Israelis obtained what they wanted."
Yet some Palestinians said the meeting had far-reaching consequences.

"President Arafat has reaped the fruits of the 'moral victory'...when he stood to hear Bibi Netanyahu asserting his government's commitment to pursue the path of peace," wrote Mohammed Hamzeh Ghanayem in al-Ayyam newspaper.
"The Likud, represented by its leader, has recognised the Palestine Liberation Organisation and the Palestinian National Authority," he wrote.
